articles.title: Why ‘Office Space’ Actor Richard Riehle Was the Quintessential Actor’s Actor (Guest Column)
articles.summary: The first time I met Richard Riehle, I was making one of the first things I’d ever made. It was a Funny or Die video, and my friend Tanner Thomason and I were trying to figure out how to get an actual actor to be in it. Someone suggested Richard. “Just offer it to him.
body: I remember arriving on set that morning and finding Richard already there, sitting by himself, reading the newspaper and drinking a root beer. He’d beaten the crew there. He didn’t need anything, didn’t seem particularly concerned that he was an actor with hundreds of credits doing a little internet video for two guys who had never really made anything before. He was just happy to be there.

He was also, without question, one of the best actors I’ve ever worked with. I know that might sound like the sort of thing people say when someone dies, but I mean it. Richard was astonishingly good. He could make a line funny just by deciding not to make it funny. He could steal a scene without seeming to do much of anything. And every once in a while he’d remind you that underneath the familiar face and the wonderful mustache was an actor with a range most people never got to see.
points: The first time I met Richard Riehle, I was making one of the first things I’d ever made.
It was a Funny or Die video, and my friend Tanner Thomason and I were trying to figure out how to get an actual actor to be in it.

articles.title: ‘Star Wars’ Comes to 2027 Super Bowl With Animated ‘Alterna-Cast’ for Disney Channel, XD, Disney+
articles.summary: Add C-3PO to the list of popular Disney personalities who will be guiding football fans through sundry telecasts of ESPN’s coverage of Super Bowl LXI in 2027. The golden droid, a mainstay of Disney’s “Star Wars” movies from Lucasfilm, will play a significant role in a real-time, animated telecast…
body: The company said it expects to unveil more details, such as visual settings, commentators and characters, in weeks to come.

Disney continues to broaden the viewing options for its airing of Super Bowl LXI, the first gridiron classic the company has had under its purview in about two decades. Earlier this month, Disney tapped outspoken host Pat McAfee to anchor “Field Pass,” a commentary-driven option, that will play alongside a traditional broadcast of the Big Game on ABC and ESPN, and a Super Bowl version of the popular “ManningCast” featuring Peyton and Eli Manning, on ESPN2. The company will offer a statistics-focused Super Bowl telecast, “Playbook,” which will be led by a team to be announced later, and air on NFL Network, as well as a Spanish-language telecast on ESPN Deportes.

A Super Bowl “mega cast” has been in consideration at the company since 2021, when Disney struck a new rights deal with the NFL that keeps “Monday Night Football” on the air at ESPN through 2033. Since that time, the league and the company have become even closer, with the league taking a 10% stake in ESPN as part of a deal that put NFL Network and NFL RedZone under the ESPN umbrella.

articles.title: Ann Hornaday, Longtime Washington Post Film Critic and Pulitzer Prize Finalist, Dies at 66
articles.summary: Ann Hornaday, the longtime film critic at The Washington Post, died Sunday at her home in Baltimore following a battle with glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer. She was 66. Hornaday spent more than 20 years at the Post, joining in 2002 and leaving in 2025. Over the course of her time at the Post,
body: Hornaday was a 2008 Pulitzer Prize finalist in criticism, submitting her review of “There Will Be Blood,” among other works, in her finalist package. She also authored “Talking Pictures,” a book about how to watch films, and before her death, a book about the filming of “All the President’s Men.”

Before Hornaday became the influential critic she is remembered as, she worked as a freelance writer in New York, contributing to publications including The New York Times and Premiere magazine. Prior to that, she worked at Ms. Magazine for two years as Gloria Steinem’s personal assistant. She was the film critic for the Baltimore Sun and the Austin American-Statesman before joining the Post.

Ann Mills Hornaday was born March 9, 1960, in Iowa City. At birth, she was adopted by William R. Hornaday Jr. and his wife, Mary Mills. Hornaday grew up in Des Moines and attended Smith College, graduating in 1982 with a major in government.
While a film critic, she was also a parishioner and Sunday school teacher in Baltimore.

articles.title: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake
articles.summary: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel.
body: ‘T he first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God, this is what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, Mad Men and DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound.

The Friday the 13th franchise has a devoted audience – and Crystal Lake’s showrunner, Brad Caleb Kane, is among them. “He’s such a fan,” says Cardellini. “I felt he would have an idea of what fans were wanting.” Kane wrote the part specifically for her, after seeing her in Netflix thriller Dead to Me, which came as a surprise. “My biggest question was, ‘How did I become the person at the front of your mind for this?’” she laughs. Did they feel any pressure in taking Friday the 13th on? “It’s daunting, but hopefully it’s an opportunity to see more of something that didn’t really get its own avenue.”
points: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis.
But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel.

articles.title: ‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US counterculture
articles.summary: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interview.
body: “Charles Manson once wrote me a letter saying, ‘If I was as powerful as you claim then you wouldn’t be here,’” Ed Sanders tells me over a video call, savouring the menace in that sentence.

Sanders is an American maverick; a musician, poet, activist, journalist and author whose greatest hit remains his bestselling 1971 book The Family, in which he chronicled the lives, crimes and trials of Manson and his followers. Sanders was well placed to report on crazed hippies, having played a pivotal role in launching the US counterculture – though he very much espoused peace, love and consciousness-raising, rather than Manson’s apocalyptic worldview.

Aged 87, Sanders is speaking with me as Fugs Film!, a feature-length documentary about the Fugs, the offbeat folk-garage-psych band Sanders initially led from 1964-69, and re-formed in the 1980s, gets its UK premiere this week. “I don’t do many interviews,” he notes. “I’m constantly approached by people requesting them. And often they are wanting access only because I knew Jimi Hendrix and Allen Ginsberg and Andy Warhol and Janis Joplin and …” He shakes his head. “Everybody now wants to make a documentary about someone I once knew.”
points: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine.

articles.title: Disney Names Carol Choi President of Asia-Pacific as Luke Kang Retires
articles.summary: The 20-year Disney veteran will take over Dec. 1, overseeing the entertainment giant’s studios, streaming, original content and consumer products businesses across the growing region.
body: In a significant leadership shake up across one of its most important international regions, Disney has appointed company veteran Carol Choi as president of Asia-Pacific following outgoing chief Luke Kang’s decision to retire.

The promotion puts Choi, a 20-year Disney veteran, at the helm of the company’s sprawling Asia-Pacific operations during a period of accelerating investment in international content and intensifying competition in the region’s still-expanding streaming markets.

Choi has held a succession of senior leadership roles since joining Disney in 2006. She previously served as managing director of the company’s Japan and South Korea businesses, following earlier positions in Greater China during the territory’s 2010s boom times. Most recently, she has overseen Disney’s regional studio operations, original content strategy and integrated marketing, playing a leading role in the expansion of Disney+ and its growing slate of Asian originals.

articles.title: Pedigree chums: why the movies are killing off fewer dogs
articles.summary: Are film-makers wary of alienating increasingly sensitive audiences by offing a pooch? Or is humanity now just too soft to deal with the trauma of a Turner & Hooch? There was a time, not so long ago, when watching a film was a clearcut experience.
body: It happened more times than you might expect. Mad Max 2, dog gets shot. Revenge, dog gets shot. Turner & Hooch, dog gets shot. Red, dog gets shot. Man with the Gun, dog gets shot. Badlands, dog gets shot. Dog Soldiers, you’ll never guess.
But how things change. These days – thanks to either political correctness gone mad or basic human decency or whatever – dogs are much less likely to be murdered in films.

A study by (of course) pet insurance firm Lassie has discovered that the number of dogs that die in movies dropped by a whopping 80% between 2020 and 2025. It reports that six years ago, 10 of the 100 highest-grossing films featured a dog dying either on or off screen. But by 2025, this number fell to just two.

Now, this could be down to any number of reasons. The first, and possibly most important, is that cinema finds itself in a perilous position. The future of the entire medium is at stake and every dollar counts, so why risk alienating a swathe of the audience by gratuitously offing a pup? Things are so bad that there is an entire website – Does the Dog Die? – purely to warn viewers of any enjoyment-spoiling canine fatalities.
points: Are film-makers wary of alienating increasingly sensitive audiences by offing a pooch?
Or is humanity now just too soft to deal with the trauma of a Turner & Hooch?
There was a time, not so long ago, when watching a film was a clearcut experience.

articles.summary: The 51-year-old faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
body: A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.

In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.
The woman told the Southwark Crown Court jury the "lad culture" of the 2000s stopped her from reporting the TV star.

articles.title: Fox Corp. Top Lawyer Adam Ciongoli Stepping Down
articles.summary: Ciongoli, who will continue as a special advisor, helped steer the company through several lawsuits involving allegations of election falsehoods. Nicholas Trutanich will take over as general counsel.
body: Adam Ciongoli is stepping down as Fox’s top lawyer. The company announced on Tuesday that he won’t renew his contract. His last day in the position is Dec. 1, after which he’ll serve as a special advisor.
At the same time, executive vice president and principal deputy general counsel Nicholas Trutanich will become general counsel. He’ll report to CEO Lachlan Murdoch.

In the position, Trutanich will navigate Fox Corp.’s $22 billion takeover of Roku. Shareholders of both companies approved the deal last week, though the Justice Department is still looking into the merger. The acquisition, if approved, would make Fox the third-largest distributor in the country by monthly viewership, according to Nielsen data. The merger is expected to be completed in the first half of next year.
“It is an exciting time of growth and innovation at FOX, and I look forward to working with colleagues across the Company to advance our goals,” Trutanich said in a statement.
points: Ciongoli, who will continue as a special advisor, helped steer the company through several lawsuits involving allegations of election falsehoods.
Nicholas Trutanich will take over as general counsel.
